transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The U.S. Supreme Court is wrestling with whether a case seeking damages over the costs of climate change should be allowed to proceed.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports on the first arguments of the new term at the High Court.
Boulder, Colorado sued Suncoran ExxonMobil to recover money for the costs of responding to global warming.
That was back in 2018, but the case has still not reached a jury.
County officials argued the companies knew but chose to deceive the public about the threats from climate change.
The energy giants are asking the Supreme Court to block the lawsuit because they say the federal government should be in charge of such a sweeping issue.
The justices asked tough questions of both sides.
They seem to be weighing a potential flood of cases in state courts against blocking cases by Boulder and other local governments at such an early stage.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
Iran says it has received a U.S. proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
There was no immediate comment from the United States.
The Iranian Speaker of the Parliament made the announcement Sunday.
More from NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchi.
Iran's Speaker of Parliament and lead negotiator Mahmoud Khalibaf said Iran received a U.S. proposal via mediators but did not provide any further details.
Khalibaf added that the U.S. had to agree to the country's conditions before any deal would be made.
Last month, Iran had put forward an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. met its terms.
President Trump rejected the plan but said he was willing to continue talks.
Many of Iran's demands mirror those in a June memorandum of understanding that fell apart a month later.
They include easing of U.S. sanctions, an end to a U.S. naval blockade, and unfreezing of Iranian assets in return for reopening the Strait.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert has died at the age of 84.
The former Illinois lawmaker was the longest-serving Republican Speaker of the House.
Whoever saw his political legacy tarnished after leaving office when he admitted in court to having sexually abused teenage boys during his years as a high school wrestling coach.
We erroneously stated that he was sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Hastert was sentenced to 15 months in federal prison for hush money payments to cover up the crimes.
Hastert's death was announced today by the coroner's office in Illinois.
The office said it was notified of Hastert's death on Saturday.
Penn America is out with a new study that reveals nearly 12,000 books were banned in public schools during the last school year.
It says that's the highest number of recorded bans in a single year since Penn America began tracking book bans in 2021.
It says the vast majority of the bans during the 2025-26 school year were in Florida and in Texas.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
The Nobel Prize in Medicine has been awarded to three scientists, one in the U.S., two in Germany,
for discoveries that help us understand how the brain works.
Dr. Karl Deisserhof says he and his colleagues, Peter Hegeman and George Nagel, figured out how to use light to control cells in the brain.
It's already been tested in human beings who are blind.
And this is a disease called retinitis pigmentosa, where there's loss of cells that's due to neurodegeneration.
And optogenetics has been used to confer light sensitivity back on these people and let them see things that they couldn't see before.
Unpasteurized milk and other raw dairy foods are unsafe to eat and can cause serious illness, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
And Piers Marie Godoy reports a new policy statement from the group says the risks are especially high for young children and people who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
The updated guidance from the AAP calls for a ban on the sale and distribution of raw milk and dairy products, including raw cheeses, because they can cause life-threatening infections.
While advocates of raw milk products say they offer health benefits, these claims are not backed by scientific evidence.
Unpasteurized dairy products can harbor pathogens like listeria, avian flu and salmonella.
This year, an outbreak of E. coli linked to raw milk cheeses resulted in 13 illnesses, including eight hospitalizations.
More than half of the people sickened were children under five years of age.
Three people developed severe kidney damage.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.
This fall, Iowa decides, and River to River will be there to tackle the issues that matter to you.
To understand what's at stake this election, I'm Ben Kiefer.
Join me as we explore what matters most to voters when it comes to life in Iowa and what candidates are proposing.
Listen to River to River, a podcast from IPR News, part of the NPR Network.
